results.title: SIMULATION EXTRAPOLATION METHOD FOR MEASUREMENT ERROR: A REVIEW - PMC
results.content: SIMEX method involves simulating several pseudo-datasets (the number of datasets simulated is denoted by B) at each level of inflation of measurement error variance λ, followed by estimation of the coefficients of covariate *W* at each level of variance inflation. If we let *Y, X, W, Z* be the response variable, true covariate, naive covariate (observed version of *X*) and another correctly measured covariate, respectively, the estimator is then considered as a function of *(Y, X, Z).* The underlying assumption for the SIMEX procedure is that measurement error variance in *X* is either known or can be estimated from data. Carroll et al., (1996) investigated the asymptotic distribution of the SIMEX estimator and also demonstrated a technique for the estimation of asymptotic standard errors for the SIMEX estimator, when the covariate *W* is subject to additive measurement error in the context of a generalized linear model. The method used to correct for the effect of measurement error in *W,* on score function estimation bears similarity to the SIMEX method in that Monte Carlo datasets are generated at a preset value of rather than being extrapolated to this value. Simulations of non-parametric regression using a sample size of 500 and specifying Laplace distribution of measurement error revealed that the SIMEX method performed well in terms of minimizing ISE along with the data driven local linear method of Delaigle, Fan, and Carroll (2008), with both outperforming the naïve estimator. Simulation studies using a Weibull AFT model (time is assumed to follow Weibull distribution) showed that the sensitivity of the SIMEX method to the approximate nature of the extrapolation function increased with increasing level of measurement error, which was evident in its lower coverage probabilities. (2017) furthered the work of McCaffrey et al., (2015) in causal inference, by investigating the use of SIMEX in estimating the correct average treatment effect (Δ), when a covariate is measured with a slightly different measurement error structure, called the mean reverting measurement error, under the doubly robust estimation assumption in the models mentioned in the previous paragraph.

results.title: Illustration of measurement error models for reducing biases in nutrition and obesity research using 2D body composition data - PMC
results.content: To illustrate the use and value of measurement error models for reducing biases when evaluating associations between body fat and having type 2 diabetes (T2D) or being physically active. Several statistical methods are available to reduce bias due to measurement error, including the classic regression calibration (RC) approach (10), multiple imputation (MI) (5, 11, 12), the maximum likelihood (ML) method (13), simulation extrapolation (SIMEX) (14, 15), and other methods (16–18). The purpose of this study was to illustrate the use and value of these methods to reduce potential biases due to measurement error when assessing the effects of body fat on two health outcomes: 1) the probability of having type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 2) the probability of being physically active (PA). In this work, three measurement error bias-adjustment techniques were applied to improve the predictions of health outcomes as estimated by BFPhoto by improving model parameters enough to yield results similar to those of the reference method, BFDXA. The SIMEX method, developed by Carroll et al (14), is a simulation-based approach that reduces the bias in parameter estimates due to measurement error by introducing random error into the model (5, 14, 15, 19). We presented and compared three measurement error bias-adjustment methods—RC, MI, and SIMEX—to reduce potential biases in statistical models used to evaluate the effect of body fat on health outcomes. The performances of these commonly used measurement error techniques were compared using body fat percentage estimated by DXA scans (BFDXA) as the reference measure and a novel 2D photographic-based method (BFPhoto) as the error-prone measure. We applied the error bias-adjustment methods to a logistic model involving body fat to predict the probability of two health outcomes: having T2D or being physically active. For example, while MI may be the most effective method for measurement error bias-adjustment in this study, the imputation procedure includes T2D and physical activity outcome variables to simulate new datasets, thus improving its accuracy. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the value of measurement error bias-adjustment methods to improve model parameters in nutrition and obesity research studies.

results.title: Measurement System Analysis and Test Method Validation: A Critical Difference - Coda Corp USA
results.content: # Measurement System Analysis and Test Method Validation: A Critical Difference. In the previous installment of the blog, we discussed our industries’ need to validate test methods in order to demonstrate that our measurement methods are capable of identifying variances inherent to production methods. The real trick to proving their suitability for use, is proving that we understand the upper limits of the potential measurement error, because the upper limit of the method uncertainty has to be added to the upper limit of the production uncertainty in order to defend the ability of the measurement system to reflect our manufacturing process in a way that is true and meaningful. Overnight it seemed that method validation programs began to consist almost solely of Gauge R&R studies. However, the number of method validation observations continued to rise, and industry representatives tasked with defending TMV programs limited to Gauge R&R studies to agency inspectors, continued to struggle. Let’s review the basic characteristics of any measurement system, which must all be addressed by a comprehensive test method validation program:. * a Gauge R&R alone is not an adequate analysis of the variance that may be inherent in a measurement system. With those points in mind, let’s ask ourselves, why we should treat developing, validating and controlling a measurement system differently than we would a process? Once these understandings are well documented and expressed in understandable process specifications and controlled via appropriate equipment operating ranges and procedures, only then can we make risk based decisions on the most appropriate experimental designs and sampling plans for each validation project, based on everything learned during the iterative development stage. It becomes easier to see when you consider the model above, and contrast it to a TMV program that is limited in scope to a Gauge R&R spreadsheet, why those programs leave Quality Management in the proverbial and unenviable position of defending why we are placing round pegs through square holes. * Review the design/development work that is the output of your local design control procedures, including Gauge R&R studies. results.title: hypothesis testing - Always use Welch-t test (unequal variances t-test) instead of Student-t or Mann-Whitney test? - Cross Validated
results.content: # Always use Welch-t test (unequal variances t-test) instead of Student-t or Mann-Whitney test? * **Welch-t test** (unequal variance t-test), if the variance of both groups might not be the same but both are still normally distributed. > If you want to compare the central tendency of 2 populations based on samples of unrelated data, then the unequal variance t-test should always be used in preference to the Student's t-test or Mann–Whitney U test. Take the ranked or unranked data and perform an unequal variance t-test. $\begingroup$ "unequal variance t-test can effectively replace the Mann–Whitney U test if the data are first ranked before the test" - what do they mean by this? For equal variances case t-test with and without Welch correction will show ~ the same result. Of course t-test without Welch correction is not correct of unequal variances case. MU test is not correct for unequal variances too BTW, but t-test and MU should undergo only limited comparison for RVs distributed in a way that mean and median is equal.
